extracted.intended_audience: inventors, designers, and small business owners seeking to file U.S. design patents (and their counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing the drawings and required components of a U.S. design patent application so the design's appearance and dimensionality are clearly communicated to the USPTO. Covers required application elements, figure descriptions, permissible specification statements, and practical advice (e.g., using a professional illustrator).

rubrics_metrics.name: Show design in many different visual perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important to show your design in many different visual perspectives. Essentially, and in order to secure a design patent, the USPTO will need you communicate your design in as many different configurations as possible such that the patent examiner can understand the dimensionality of your design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include multiple elevations, cross-sections, and perspective views (e.g., top, bottom, left/right side, front elevation, perspective, cross-sectional/proximal/distal/transversal views). The article emphasizes that showing dimensionality and perspective is often harder and more important than one might think for typical three-dimensional objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble (required application element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preamble, stating name of the applicant, title of the design, and a brief description of the nature and intended use of the article in which the design is embodied;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include applicant name, design title, and brief description of the article and intended use in the application preamble as a required element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-reference to related applications (when applicable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-reference to related applications (unless included in the application data sheet);
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include cross-references to any related prior applications or rely on the application data sheet to provide this information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement regarding federally sponsored research or development
rubrics_metrics.description: Statement regarding federally sponsored research or development;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the design was developed with federal sponsorship, include the appropriate statement in the application as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description of the figure(s) of the drawing
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of the figure(s) of the drawing;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide figure descriptions that indicate what view each drawing represents (e.g., front elevation, top plan, perspective view). These descriptions label views so the examiner understands each illustration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature description
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe notable features of the design as needed. While drawings are primary, brief feature descriptions can help clarify particular elements of the design.

rubrics_metrics.name: A single claim (design patents)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design patent applications should include only one claim. The page reiterates that design patents typically include a single claim and that this is the standard practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings or photographs
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include clear drawings or, where permitted, photographs that fully disclose the claimed design from the necessary viewpoints. Ensure images meet USPTO form/quality requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executed oath or declaration
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a signed oath or declaration executed by the inventor(s) as part of the application filing requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figure descriptions are generally the design's best enabling description
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent figure description indicates what view of the drawing is represented by the image drawn (i.e., front elevation, top plan, perspective view, etc.). Any description of the design in the specification, other than a brief description of the drawing, is generally not required as the drawings are the design's best enabling description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep specification text minimal—normally a brief description of the figures suffices. Special, longer descriptions are sometimes helpful for complex drawings but are not usually necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible additional specification statements
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to the figure descriptions, the following types of statements are permissible in a design patent specification: a description of the appearance of portions of the claimed design which are not illustrated in the drawing disclosure (i.e., 'the right side elevational view is a mirror image of the left side'); description disclaiming portions of the article not shown, that form no part of the claimed design; statement indicating that any broken line illustration of environmental structure in the drawing is not part of the design sought to be patented; and description denoting the nature and environmental use of the claimed design, if not included in the preamble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these permitted statements to: (1) note mirrored views, (2) disclaim unclaimed parts, (3) clarify broken-line environmental elements are not claimed, and (4) state the nature/environmental use if not in the preamble. These help avoid overclaiming or ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent drawings must follow USPTO/formal rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent drawings are required by patent office rules to be in a particular form, and that is why you want to work with a professional patent illustrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure drawings meet USPTO formal requirements (format, line quality, shading, margins, numbering, broken/solid lines usage, etc.). Non-conforming drawings can lead to rejections or require replacement drawings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a professional patent illustrator and attorney guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent attorney will not typically create your patent illustrations, but they will help guide the creation as the patent illustrator will work under the direction of the patent attorneys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage a professional patent illustrator to produce compliant drawings; coordinate with a patent attorney who will direct the illustrator to ensure legal sufficiency and compliance with examiner expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design must be novel/distinctive relative to public domain
rubrics_metrics.description: The legal protection given to a visual or graphic work requires that items or designs not be substantially similar in concept to what is already in the public domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify novelty and distinctiveness before filing — if the design is not sufficiently unique compared to existing designs or public-domain items, the chances of obtaining a design patent decrease significantly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broken lines to show environment and disclaim them when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Statement indicating that any broken line illustration of environmental structure in the drawing is not part of the design sought to be patented;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use broken lines in drawings to depict environment/unnclaimed structure and include an explicit statement that such broken-line elements are not part of the claimed design to avoid unintentional claim scope.
